TITLE INSURANCE AND THE PRELIMINARY REPORT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St, Springfield, CA · Pat Morgan

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes what California law says about title insurance and about the preliminary report (also called a commitment or binder) that a title company issues before a policy is written. It is prepared for reference in connection with the property at 123 Main St, Springfield, CA, in a transaction between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee in which title work is being handled by Valley Title Company. The sheet collects the definitions in the Insurance Code, the statutory rules on rate filing, referral inducements and escrow disbursement that apply to title insurers, and the holdings of the California decisions construing those provisions. It does not examine or evaluate the title to 123 Main St, Springfield, CA, does not interpret any preliminary report, commitment or policy issued in this transaction, does not assess Valley Title Company's compliance with any statute, and does not recommend whether or in what amount any coverage should be obtained.

WHAT THE INSURANCE CODE MEANS BY "TITLE INSURANCE" AND "TITLE POLICY"
The Insurance Code defines title insurance by reference to three insured risks: liens or encumbrances on, or defects in, the title; invalidity or unenforceability of liens or encumbrances; and incorrectness of searches relating to title. A "title policy" is defined simply as the written instrument or contract by which title insurance liability is assumed. The California courts describe the resulting relationship as one of indemnity: in Lawrence v. Chicago Title Ins. Co. the Court of Appeal stated that title insurance is a contract for indemnity under which the insurer is obligated to indemnify the insured against losses sustained if a specific contingency, such as the discovery of a lien or encumbrance affecting title, occurs.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-15]
  "“Title insurance” means insuring, guaranteeing or indemnifying owners of real or personal property or the holders of liens or encumbrances thereon or others interested therein against loss or damage suffered by reason of: (a) Liens or encumbrances on, or defects in the title to said property; (b) Invalidity or unenforceability of any liens or encumbrances thereon; or (c) Incorrectness of searches relating to the title to real or personal property."
  — Cal. Ins. Code § 12340.1, Insurance Code § 12340.1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=INS&sectionNum=12340.1.)
  "“Title policy” means any written instrument or contract by means of which title insurance liability is assumed."
  — Cal. Ins. Code § 12340.2, Insurance Code § 12340.2 (https://law.onecle.com/california/insurance/12340.2.html)
  "Title insurance is a contract for indemnity under which the insurer is obligated to indemnify the insured against losses sustained in the event that a specific contingency, e.g., the discovery of a lien or encumbrance affecting title, occurs."
  — Lawrence v. Chicago Title Ins. Co., 192 Cal.App.3d 70, 74 (1987) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2107472/lawrence-v-chicago-title-insurance/)

The standard owner's and lender's forms in general use in California are private forms filed with the Insurance Commissioner under Section 12401.1 and are not reproduced in the code, so nothing in this clause states what any policy issued for 123 Main St, Springfield, CA covers or excludes. WHO MAY TRANSACT TITLE INSURANCE: TITLE INSURERS AND UNDERWRITTEN TITLE COMPANIES
The Insurance Code separates the company that assumes the risk from the company that does the searching. An "underwritten title company" is defined as a corporation engaged in preparing title searches, examinations, reports, certificates or abstracts on the basis of which a title insurer writes policies. The "business of title insurance" is defined to include not only issuing policies but also the performance by a title insurer, an underwritten title company or a controlled escrow company of any service in conjunction with the issuance or contemplated issuance of a title policy, expressly including the handling of an escrow, settlement or closing. Section 12360 states a monoline rule: an insurer that anywhere in the United States transacts any class of insurance other than title insurance is ineligible for a certificate of authority to transact title insurance in California, or for renewal of one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-15]

  "The performance by a title insurer, an underwritten title company or a controlled escrow company of any service in conjunction with the issuance or contemplated issuance of a title policy including but not limited to the handling of any escrow, settlement or closing in connection therewith"

WHAT A PRELIMINARY REPORT IS UNDER SECTION 12340.11 — AND WHAT AN ABSTRACT OF TITLE IS
Since 1982 the Insurance Code has defined the preliminary report by what it is not. Section 12340.11 provides that a "preliminary report," "commitment" or "binder" is a report furnished in connection with an application for title insurance and is an offer to issue a title policy subject to the stated exceptions, that such reports are not abstracts of title, and that none of the rights, duties or responsibilities attaching to the preparation and issuance of an abstract of title attach to their issuance. The same section states that such a report is not to be construed as, and does not constitute, a representation as to the condition of title, but constitutes a statement of the terms and conditions on which the issuer is willing to issue its policy. Section 12340.10 defines the separate document, the abstract of title, as a written representation provided pursuant to a contract, intended to be relied upon by the person who contracted for it, listing the recorded instruments that impart constructive notice with respect to the chain of title; it adds that an abstract of title is not a title policy.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-15]
  "“Preliminary report”, “commitment”, or “binder” are reports furnished in connection with an application for title insurance and are offers to issue a title policy subject to the stated exceptions set forth in the reports and such other matters as may be incorporated by reference therein. The reports are not abstracts of title, nor are any of the rights, duties or responsibilities applicable to the preparation and issuance of an abstract of title applicable to the issuance of any report."
  — Cal. Ins. Code § 12340.11, Insurance Code § 12340.11 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=INS&sectionNum=12340.11.)
  "Any such report shall not be construed as, nor constitute, a representation as to the condition of title to real property, but shall constitute a statement of the terms and conditions upon which the issuer is willing to issue its title policy, if such offer is accepted."
  — Cal. Ins. Code § 12340.11 (second sentence), Insurance Code § 12340.11 (https://law.onecle.com/california/insurance/12340.11.html)
  "“Abstract of title” is a written representation, provided pursuant to a contract, whether written or oral, intended to be relied upon by the person who has contracted for the receipt of such representation, listing all recorded conveyances, instruments or documents which, under the laws of this state, impart constructive notice with respect to the chain of title to the real property described therein. An abstract of title is not a title policy as defined in Section 12340.2."
  — Cal. Ins. Code § 12340.10, Insurance Code § 12340.10 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=INS&sectionNum=12340.10.)

The statute speaks to preliminary reports, commitments and binders, and does not by its terms address guarantee products such as a litigation guarantee or a trustee's sale guarantee, which the corpus does not cover. HOW THE COURTS READ THE 1981 STATUTES: SOUTHLAND TITLE CORP. V. SUPERIOR COURT
Southland Title Corp. v. Superior Court is the decision that first gave the 1981 statutes their operative effect. The Court of Appeal held that the Legislature had drawn a formal distinction between an abstract of title and a policy of title insurance, and described the preliminary report, for which little or no charge is made, as merely the inducement to purchase a title policy, no longer to be treated or considered to have the legal consequence of an abstract of title; the court added that if a current representation as to the status of title is required, an abstract can be ordered and separately purchased. The court read Section 12340.10 as making clear that a person who contracts for the written representation known as an abstract of title receives all the rights associated with that representation, and that such a purchased and express representation can be relied upon. Answering the argument that buyers and sellers in practice continue to order and rely on preliminary reports, the court stated that it is now clear that such reliance cannot be justified and is done only at a party's peril.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-15]
  "A preliminary report, for which little or no charge is made, is merely the inducement to purchase a title policy. It will no longer be treated or considered to have the legal consequence of an abstract of title. If a current representation as to the status of title is required then an abstract can be ordered and separately purchased."
  — Southland Title Corp. v. Superior Court, 231 Cal.App.3d 530, 536 (1991) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2118849/southland-title-corp-v-superior-court/)
  "The effect of section 12340.10 is to make clear that a person who contracts for the written representation known as an “abstract of title” will receive all of the rights associated with that written representation. Such a purchased and express representation can be relied upon."
  — Southland Title Corp. v. Superior Court, 231 Cal.App.3d 530, 536 (1991) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2118849/southland-title-corp-v-superior-court/)

WHOSE BENEFIT THE TITLE SEARCH SERVES: SIEGEL V. FIDELITY NATIONAL TITLE INS. CO.
Siegel v. Fidelity National Title Ins. Co. explains the reasoning behind the statutory scheme. The Court of Appeal stated that the function of title insurance is to protect against the possibility that liens and other items not found in the search or disclosed in the preliminary report exist, and that in enacting Sections 12340.10 and 12340.11 the Legislature recognized that no reliance should ever be placed on a preliminary report or a policy of title insurance to show the condition of title. Summarizing, the court stated that a title insurer prepares a preliminary report to limit its own risk, by locating and excluding items from coverage, and not on behalf of any party to a real estate transaction, and that a party who does not purchase title insurance may not rely on the title insurer to protect that party's interests or to disclose all detrimental information contained in the recorded files.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-15]

  "In enacting Insurance Code sections 12340.10 and 12340.11, the Legislature recognized that no reliance should ever be placed on a preliminary report or a policy of title insurance to show the condition of title."

A party who does not purchase title insurance may not rely on the title insurer to protect his or her interests or to disclose all detrimental information contained in the recorded files."

THE TWO DOCUMENTS THAT CARRY A RIGHT OF RELIANCE: SOIFER V. CHICAGO TITLE CO.
Soifer v. Chicago Title Co. extended Southland to an informal request for title information. The plaintiff, a foreclosure-sale investor, had asked a title company for quick answers about lien seniority without buying either a policy or an abstract, and sued when an answer proved wrong. Restating its earlier holding, the same division of the Court of Appeal said that if a representation was sought from the title company as to the condition of title to a particular property, an abstract of title should have been obtained. The court stated that a party that seeks to hold an insurer liable for negligently providing title information upon which the party relied must obtain an abstract of title, and that there are two ways in which an interested party can obtain title information upon which reliance may be placed: an abstract of title or a policy of title insurance.

WHAT THE POLICY ITSELF DOES AND DOES NOT SUPPORT: LAWRENCE V. CHICAGO TITLE INS. CO.
Lawrence v. Chicago Title Ins. Co. addressed a lender whose insured deed of trust turned out to be in third rather than second position. The Court of Appeal held that because the policy of title insurance does not constitute a representation that the insured-against contingency will not occur, when that contingency occurs no action for negligence or negligent misrepresentation will lie against the insurer based upon the policy of title insurance alone; the insurer's obligation is to indemnify on the policy's terms. On the separate question of the preliminary report, the court stated that even if a preliminary report constitutes a representation of title on which the recipient is entitled to rely, a claim of negligence must be predicated upon the insured's actual reliance on the report, and it affirmed summary judgment where the plaintiffs had not seen the report before funding the loan.

REPORTS ISSUED BEFORE 1982: WHITE V. WESTERN TITLE INS. CO. AND THE ABSTRACTOR RULE
Before Section 12340.11 took effect the California courts treated a title insurer furnishing a preliminary report as an abstractor of title, with a duty to list all matters of public record. In White v. Western Title Ins. Co. the Supreme Court applied that rule to a report that omitted a recorded water easement, and rejected the insurer's reliance on disclaimer language, stating that a title company is engaged in a business affected with the public interest and cannot, by an adhesory contract, exculpate itself from liability for negligence. The court also rejected the argument that the newly enacted Section 12340.11 governed, holding that nothing in the language or legislative history of the section suggests an intention to apply it to a preliminary title report procured prior to its effective date.

WHETHER A TITLE INSURER MUST AGREE TO INSURE: QUELIMANE CO. V. STEWART TITLE GUARANTY CO.
Quelimane Co. v. Stewart Title Guaranty Co. considered whether title insurers owe a duty to issue policies on property whose chain of title includes a tax deed. The Supreme Court agreed with the Court of Appeal that the negligence cause of action failed, stating that while title insurers may not discriminate among purchasers on the basis of race, ethnicity, religion, gender or other personal characteristics, citing Civil Code section 51, they may opt to limit their potential liability by declining certain risks without violating any statutory or common law obligation. The court found no special relationship giving rise to a duty to issue a policy of title insurance to a member of the public purchasing tax-defaulted property from the plaintiffs.

FILED RATES: SECTIONS 12401.1 AND 12401.7
Title insurance rates in California are filed rates. Section 12401.1 requires every title insurer, underwritten title company and controlled escrow company to file with the Insurance Commissioner its schedules of rates, all regularly issued forms of title policies to which those rates apply, and every proposed modification; the schedule filed by a title insurer must set out the entire charge to the public for each type of policy, including without separate statement the portion attributable to work performed by an underwritten title company, and each filing takes effect no earlier than the thirtieth day after the Commissioner receives it. Section 12401.7 bars use of a rate before its effective date, and before the filing has been publicly displayed and made readily available to the public for at least 30 days in each of the filer's offices in the county to which the rate applies; it also provides that no rate increase applies to title policies or services contracted for before the effective date.

expectedJSON.body: Lawrence v. Chicago Title Ins. Co. addressed a lender whose insured deed of trust turned out to be in third rather than second position. The Court of Appeal held that because the policy of title insurance does not constitute a representation that the insured-against contingency will not occur, when that contingency occurs no action for negligence or negligent misrepresentation will lie against the insurer based upon the policy of title insurance alone; the insurer's obligation is to indemnify on the policy's terms. On the separate question of the preliminary report, the court stated that even if a preliminary report constitutes a representation of title on which the recipient is entitled to rely, a claim of negligence must be predicated upon the insured's actual reliance on the report, and it affirmed summary judgment where the plaintiffs had not seen the report before funding the loan.

citations.quote: Accordingly, when such contingency occurs, no action for negligence or negligent misrepresentation will lie against the insurer based upon the policy of title insurance alone.

expectedJSON.body: Before Section 12340.11 took effect the California courts treated a title insurer furnishing a preliminary report as an abstractor of title, with a duty to list all matters of public record. In White v. Western Title Ins. Co. the Supreme Court applied that rule to a report that omitted a recorded water easement, and rejected the insurer's reliance on disclaimer language, stating that a title company is engaged in a business affected with the public interest and cannot, by an adhesory contract, exculpate itself from liability for negligence. The court also rejected the argument that the newly enacted Section 12340.11 governed, holding that nothing in the language or legislative history of the section suggests an intention to apply it to a preliminary title report procured prior to its effective date.

expectedJSON.body: Quelimane Co. v. Stewart Title Guaranty Co. considered whether title insurers owe a duty to issue policies on property whose chain of title includes a tax deed. The Supreme Court agreed with the Court of Appeal that the negligence cause of action failed, stating that while title insurers may not discriminate among purchasers on the basis of race, ethnicity, religion, gender or other personal characteristics, citing Civil Code section 51, they may opt to limit their potential liability by declining certain risks without violating any statutory or common law obligation. The court found no special relationship giving rise to a duty to issue a policy of title insurance to a member of the public purchasing tax-defaulted property from the plaintiffs.

expectedJSON.body: Section 12414.26 provides that no act done, action taken or agreement made pursuant to the authority conferred by Article 5.5, on rate filing, or Article 5.7, on advisory organizations, constitutes a violation of or grounds for prosecution or civil proceedings under any other California law that does not specifically refer to insurance. In Quelimane the Court of Appeal had read that section, together with Section 12414.29, as exempting title insurers from the Cartwright Act and the unfair competition law. The Supreme Court disagreed. It held that the scope of these sections is expressly limited to articles 5.5 and 5.7 of division 2, part 6, of the Insurance Code, and that the sentence in Section 12414.29 about exclusive regulation, read with its closing words about local regulation or ordinance, shows that the legislative purpose was to preempt local regulation, not to exempt title insurers from other state laws governing unfair business practices.

expectedJSON.body: Title insurance rates in California are filed rates. Section 12401.1 requires every title insurer, underwritten title company and controlled escrow company to file with the Insurance Commissioner its schedules of rates, all regularly issued forms of title policies to which those rates apply, and every proposed modification; the schedule filed by a title insurer must set out the entire charge to the public for each type of policy, including without separate statement the portion attributable to work performed by an underwritten title company, and each filing takes effect no earlier than the thirtieth day after the Commissioner receives it. Section 12401.7 bars use of a rate before its effective date, and before the filing has been publicly displayed and made readily available to the public for at least 30 days in each of the filer's offices in the county to which the rate applies; it also provides that no rate increase applies to title policies or services contracted for before the effective date.

citations.quote: Every title insurer, underwritten title company, and controlled escrow company shall file with the commissioner its schedules of rates, all regularly issued forms of title policies to which such rates apply, and every modification thereof which it proposes to use in this state.

No title insurer, underwritten title company or controlled escrow company shall use any rate in the business of title insurance prior to its effective date nor prior to the filing with respect to such rate having been publicly displayed and made readily available to the public for a period of no less than 30 days in each office of the title insurer, underwritten title company, or controlled escrow company in the county to which such rate applies, and no rate increase shall apply to title policies or services which have been contracted for prior to such effective date.

expectedJSON.body: Section 12404 makes it unlawful for a title insurer, underwritten title company or controlled escrow company to pay, directly or indirectly, any commission, compensation or other consideration to any person as an inducement for the placement or referral of title business, and states that actual placement or referral is not a precondition to a violation. The section then lists activities deemed per se unlawful inducements, among them paying, furnishing or providing — or offering to do so — assistance with another person's business expenses, a category the statute illustrates with rent, employee salaries, furniture, copiers, facsimile machines, automobiles, telephone services or equipment, and computers. "Person" is defined for this purpose to reach owners and prospective owners, lessees, obligees and their agents, representatives, attorneys and employees.

expectedJSON.body: Where the title entity also holds the escrow, Section 12413.1 fixes the earliest day funds may leave the escrow account. The section states that no title insurance company, controlled escrow company or underwritten title company shall disburse funds from an escrow account until the day established by the subdivisions that follow, which key the timing to the availability schedules of Part 229 of Title 12 of the Code of Federal Regulations as those regulations existed on January 1, 1990. Deposits accorded next-day availability may not be disbursed until the business day after deposit; deposits not accorded next-day availability wait until the federal regulation requires the funds be made available; and funds deposited by cash or by electronic payment may be disbursed on the same business day as the deposit. Separate subdivisions address drafts submitted for collection, written confirmation of final settlement, a bona fide error defense, and recording before funds are available where the parties consent in writing beforehand.
